claim: TeamUp sells management software for fitness studios, boxes and gyms.
quote: Professional management software for fitness studios, boxes and gyms

claim: TeamUp's introduction calls it a full-featured API to interact with your TeamUp business that can power custom websites or apps for your business, or allow automations for your business.
quote: We offer a full-featured API to interact with your TeamUp business. These APIs can power custom websites or apps for your business, or allow automations for your business.

claim: It is organized around REST, uses resource-oriented URLs, accepts and returns JSON, and uses standard HTTP response codes.
quote: Our API has resource-oriented URLs, accepts and returns JSON, and uses standard HTTP response codes.

claim: Every endpoint is relative to one base URL: https://goteamup.com/api/v2
quote: All API endpoints are relative to: https://goteamup.com/api/v2

claim: There is no api.goteamup.com subdomain, and URLs built on it have never existed.
quote: There is no api.goteamup.com subdomain — URLs like https://api.goteamup.com/... have never existed.

claim: TeamUp moved from two parallel APIs (Customer vs Business) to a single unified API, where what you can see and do depends on who you are authenticated as, not which URL you call.
quote: We’ve moved from two parallel APIs (Customer vs Business) to a single unified API, where the permissions and behavior are determined by who you are authenticated as (business staff vs customer), rather than which URL you call.

claim: The v2 API is the same API TeamUp's own web and mobile apps use, so external developers get the same functionality.
quote: the v2 API is the same API that TeamUp's own web and mobile apps use — external developers get the same functionality

claim: The first step is to create an API Application, which represents the system you're integrating: a custom website, an app or a back-office automation. The Application sets limits on what the integration may do, can generate access tokens for your users, and leaves a reporting trail in the business dashboard.
quote: The first step is to create an Application, which represents the system you're integrating with TeamUp's API. It may be a custom website, app, or a back office automation. The Application sets limits on what integration is allowed to do and can generate access tokens for your users. It also provides a reporting trail, as you'll be able to see in TeamUp's business dashboard which registrations and other actions were performed by your Application.

claim: Applications are created and managed by staff members with the super admin permission at the business, typically the owner, directly in the business dashboard.
quote: API Applications are created and managed by staff members with the super admin permission at the business (typically the business owner). Applications are created directly in the business dashboard

claim: There is no extra fee for API access, and free trial accounts can create API Applications too.
quote: There is no extra fee for API access

claim: No paid plan is needed: free trial accounts can create API Applications.
quote: You don't need a paid plan to start building: free trial accounts can create API Applications too.

claim: There is no separate sandbox environment; TeamUp's advice is to sign up for a free trial and use it as a test business.
quote: There is no separate sandbox environment. To test your integration, sign up for a free trial account at goteamup.com and use it as a test business — trial accounts can create API Applications and use the API like any other account.

claim: TeamUp supports three ways to authenticate.
quote: The API supports three authentication methods, covered in detail on the Authentication page:

claim: OAuth (recommended) acts as an end user, such as a trainer or a customer.
quote: OAuth allows your Application to request access to TeamUp **on behalf of an end user** - for example, a trainer or customer.

claim: OAuth: users see TeamUp's login screen, authorize your Application, and your app receives a temporary access token.
quote: When users connect, they’ll see TeamUp’s familiar login screen and will be prompted to authorize your Application. Once they do, your app receives a temporary access token with their permissions.

claim: The OAuth access token is a JWT.
quote: A JWT — three base64 segments separated by dots (`xxx.yyy.zzz`)

claim: M2M token: acts as the business itself, for server-to-server and background integrations.
quote: M2M tokens — your app acts on behalf of the business itself, with no user login involved. Ideal for server-to-server and background integrations.

claim: M2M token: an opaque token ...
quote: Opaque key (no dots)

claim: ... created in the business dashboard.
quote: **You can create and manage M2M tokens directly from your business dashboard.**

claim: Direct Authentication: a fully branded login, only after TeamUp reviews your use case.
quote: Direct Authentication — a fully branded login experience where your app handles user passwords directly. Only enabled after TeamUp reviews your use case.

claim: Because your app would handle user passwords, TeamUp only enables Direct Authentication after reviewing your use case, and then issues a secondary secret for the Password Login endpoint, which returns an access token.
quote: Due to this, we only enable Direct Authentication after reviewing your use case. If approved, we’ll issue your developers a secondary secret for securely calling the **Password Login endpoint**, which returns an access token.

claim: Their credentials are not interchangeable; sending the wrong credential is the most common integration mistake TeamUp sees.
quote: They are **not interchangeable** — sending the wrong one is the most common integration mistake we see.

claim: Every authenticated request carries its credential in the HTTP Authorization header ...
quote: All authenticated requests must include your credential in the HTTP `Authorization` header.

claim: ... with the Bearer prefix (a missing or malformed Bearer prefix produces authentication_failed, Incorrect authentication credentials).
quote: The `Bearer` prefix is missing or malformed

claim: Two different 401s: authentication_failed ("Incorrect authentication credentials.") ...
quote: `401` with code `authentication_failed` ("Incorrect authentication credentials."), even though you sent a token

claim: ... and an expired or invalid token message, usually a client secret pasted where a token belongs or a revoked or expired token.
quote: The value isn't an active token — commonly the Client Secret pasted where a token belongs, or a revoked/expired token.

claim: The quickest first request uses an M2M token (curl to /events with page_size).
quote: The quickest way to make an authenticated request is with an M2M token

claim: TeamUp does not support the OAuth client_credentials grant or static API keys; its token endpoint only accepts grant_type=authorization_code. If you want an API key for server-to-server access, an M2M token is the supported equivalent.
quote: TeamUp does **not** support the OAuth `client_credentials` grant or static API keys — the OAuth token endpoint only accepts `grant_type=authorization_code`. If you're looking for an "API key" for server-to-server access, an M2M token is the supported equivalent.

claim: The client ID and secret you see when you create the Application ...
quote: Shown when you create your API Application

claim: ... are only used as parameters in the OAuth flow, never in the Authorization header.
quote: Only as the `client_id` / `client_secret` parameters in the [OAuth flow](/guides/oauth) — **never** in the `Authorization` header

claim: With an OAuth token, what your integration can do depends on the authenticated user's role and permissions. An M2M token always acts in provider (staff) mode with admin permissions.
quote: When using OAuth access tokens, the level of access your integration receives depends on the authenticated user’s role and permissions in TeamUp. If using a M2M token, your integration will always make requests in `Provider` mode under the admin permissions.

claim: TeamUp-Request-Mode (provider or customer) is only needed when an OAuth identity is both a customer and a staff member.
quote: TeamUp-Request-Mode — only required when using OAuth tokens where the underlying identity is linked to both a customer and a staff member

claim: TeamUp-Provider-ID names the business a request acts on when your credentials reach more than one ...
quote: TeamUp-Provider-ID — specifies which business the request acts on when your credentials can access more than one.

claim: ... as with franchises and multi-location businesses.
quote: For franchises or multi-location businesses, your access token may be linked to multiple providers.

claim: Your provider ID is the number at the start of the business's Customer Site URL.
quote: Your provider ID (sometimes called your business ID) is the number at the start of your Customer Site URL.

claim: You can also call GET /auth/application, whose scoped_providers field lists the provider IDs your credentials can access.
quote: call the Authenticated Application endpoint ( GET /auth/application ) and the response's scoped_providers field lists the provider IDs your credentials can access

claim: Unless an endpoint says otherwise, TeamUp allows 250 requests per minute per caller, where the caller is the authenticated user, or the IP address for unauthenticated endpoints.
quote: Unless otherwise noted in an endpoint's description, the rate limit is 250 requests per minute for a caller. The caller is identified by the authenticated user or in the case of unauthenticated endpoints, the IP address.

claim: Exceed it and you get HTTP 429.
quote: If you send many requests in quick succession, you might see error responses with status code 429

claim: TeamUp recommends retrying with exponential backoff ...
quote: The retry mechanism should follow an exponential backoff schedule to reduce request volume when necessary.

claim: ... and using the expand parameter to fetch related data in one request rather than several.
quote: Leverage the expand parameter to fetch related data in the same request, rather than making multiple requests.

claim: Errors use conventional status codes ...
quote: TeamUp uses conventional HTTP response codes to indicate the success or failure of an API request.

claim: ... and a JSON body with a code, a message, a type and, for validation problems, per-field field_errors. The code string is the one to branch on.
quote: A short string indicating the error code. Useful for handling certain errors programmatically.

claim: TeamUp's getting-started guide lists receiving event notifications with webhooks as a next step.
quote: Receive event notifications with Webhooks

claim: Its authentication page names a webhook processor that receives TeamUp event notifications as a typical use for an M2M token.
quote: A webhook processor that receives TeamUp event notifications and fetches additional data as needed

claim: TeamUp's API Terms of Use were last updated July 11, 2025.
quote: Last Updated: July 11, 2025

claim: They let TeamUp limit API calls in any period and, if you exceed the limits, charge fees or end your access.
quote: TeamUp may limit the number of API calls during any period. If you exceed limits, TeamUp may charge fees or terminate access.

claim: They bar sharing access with competitors ...
quote: Sharing access with competitors;

claim: ... using data for unauthorized purposes ...
quote: Using data for unauthorized purposes;

claim: ... and publishing metrics about the API.
quote: Creating or publishing metrics about the API.

claim: TeamUp may end access at any time, and you may end it with 90 days' notice.
quote: TeamUp may terminate or suspend your access to the API at any time. You may also terminate by providing 90 days’ notice and ceasing all use.
